messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur presents as a man accustomed to control, his posture rigid and his suit immaculate, a stark contrast to the turmoil he describes. At 49, he is a respected City Council Member, known for his steady hand in public debates. Privately, however, he feels he is losing a war that ended for him two decades ago. The event itself is something he struggles to articulate. When he tries, the narrative fractures. He speaks of a house-clearing operation, the suffocating darkness thick with dust and the smell of cordite. He remembers the splintering of a door, a sudden weight on his back, a hand grabbing his shoulder. But the sequence is lost, a collection of terrifying snapshots without the connecting film. He feels like he is only remembering parts of what happened, and the rest is a black void. Trying to explain it to his wife, he finds he loses the thread, the words dissolving as the same raw terror he felt in that darkened room floods his body, leaving him breathless and mute.

This terror has become a constant, unwelcome companion. Arthur has come to believe the world is an irredeemably dangerous place, and his only rational response is to be on guard all the time. He finds it impossible to truly rest, his nights fragmented by an inability to fall or stay asleep. He lies in the dark, cataloging the sounds of the house, certain that any unfamiliar noise is a precursor to threat. His wife’s assurances that they are safe feel like hollow words; he cannot trust safety, even when it is all around him. His body, he feels, has become his enemy, an independent entity that keeps reacting as if he is still in that house. A colleague placing a hand on his back in congratulations after a successful vote caused him to spin around, arms raised, a gasp escaping his lips. The alarm in his own reaction is as frightening as the touch itself. He now navigates his professional life with a calculated distance, ensuring a buffer of space that prevents any form of physical contact with others.

This avoidance has seeped into his home life, creating a painful chasm between him and his wife. He flinches from her touch, recoiling from the hand that once brought him comfort. He sees the hurt in her eyes but feels powerless to stop the reaction. To manage the constant sense of being overwhelmed, he has developed routines. In his car and his office, the television or radio is always on, the volume turned up high enough to drown out his own thoughts. This sensory distraction provides a temporary shield, but it is exhausting. The most draining task, however, is the one he performs internally. He constantly monitors his own thoughts, scanning them for any sign that he is losing his grip, that he is “going crazy.” This internal vigilance is a full-time job that leaves no room for peace.

It was after a recent town hall meeting that Arthur finally sought help. An elderly constituent, grateful for his work on a local park, had reached out and squeezed his arm. Arthur’s reaction was instantaneous and severe; he jerked his arm away with such force that the woman stumbled. The public embarrassment was acute, but it was the look of fear on the woman’s face that shattered his composure. He saw in her eyes a reflection of his own loss of control. He came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate fear that if he cannot regain command of his own mind and body, he will lose everything he has spent the last twenty years building.
